title: Tyre to the Pyre: the Wanderer Who Built Carthage
years: c. 850-814 BC (historical/legendary reign); with the poets' fold of the Aeneas years, traditionally c. 1182-1180 BC
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Tyre, the Wound at the Root

stops.name: Tyre, a daughter of the house of Belus
stops.campa: Tyre stands on her rock in the sea, mistress of the purple dye-vats and the cedar road to Egypt, when a daughter is born to the king the Tyrians call Belus, or Mattan. The priests name her Elissa; later ages, remembering how far she wandered, will call her Dido, 'the wanderer.' She grows up under the bell of Melqart's temple and the reek of the murex pits, clever, pious, and already marked, the annals say, as fit to rule better than any woman, or most men, of her house.
suggested_refs: The rock-island city of Tyre (Sur), Lebanon, mother-port of the Phoenician diaspora
sources: Josephus, Against Apion 1.18 (quoting Menander of Ephesus on the Tyrian king-list)

stops.name: Tyre, the death of Belus, the throne given to Pygmalion
stops.campa: The old king dies and leaves the throne of Tyre to his son and daughter jointly, but the people will not be governed by a woman and set the boy Pygmalion, still a child, alone on the seat. Elissa does not contest it. She takes the immense dowry of her house instead and gives her hand to Acerbas, her own uncle, priest of Melqart-Hercules, a man of such fortune that he trusts no wall to hold it and buries the greater part of his gold in the earth, telling no one but her.
suggested_refs: The Tyrian king-list of Menander of Ephesus, preserved in Josephus

stops.name: Tyre, the altar, and the murder of Acerbas
stops.campa: Pygmalion, grown to manhood and hungry for gold beyond what a kingdom yields, learns of his brother-in-law's buried hoard and is seized, the histories say, by a greed that puts out every family feeling. He strikes Acerbas down in secret, before the very altars of the god he serves, and thinks the killing hidden, for Elissa is his sister, and he trusts her grief to be private and her silence assured. He has not reckoned with what a wronged wife can do with a fleet, a treasury, and half the senate of Tyre behind her.
suggested_refs: Melqart's temple at Tyre, the murdered priest's own altar
sources: Virgil, Aeneid 1.340-352 (the murder 'ante aras,' before the altars)

stops.name: Tyre, the ghost of Sychaeus reveals the gold and the crime
stops.campa: Where the histories give her cunning, the poets give her a vision: the unburied ghost of her husband, Sychaeus in the Roman telling, comes to her in sleep, lifts the veil from his own wounds, and lays bare the altar's crime and her brother's hand in it. He shows her ancient treasure hidden in the earth, a weight of gold and silver known to no one else alive, and tells her to take it and flee the country. She wakes knowing what must be done, and grieves alone, trusting no face at court, not even her own reflection.
stops.quote: Auxiliumque viae veteres tellure recludit / thesauros, ignotum argenti pondus et auri.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 1.358-359 (the ghost unearths the ancient hoard, 'an unknown weight of silver and gold')
suggested_refs: The ghost of Sychaeus revealing the buried gold, a recurring motif in Renaissance Dido cycles

stops.name: Tyre, the sacks of sand and the gathering of the conspirators
stops.campa: Elissa feigns reconciliation, tells her brother she wishes to move into his own house so the sight of her husband's rooms will no longer grieve her, and asks for men to help the removal. By night she loads bags of common sand aboard the waiting ships, calling them Acerbas's gold, and has them cast into the sea as an offering to appease his shade, so that the attendants, thinking themselves already accomplices in a fortune thrown to the deep, dare not turn back to Pygmalion. She wins over the frightened men and a company of the city's senators to sail with her before dawn.
stops.quote: That he would favourably receive his wealth which he had left behind him, and accept that as an offering to his shade.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.4 (trans. J. S. Watson; her entreaty to Acerbas as the sand goes into the sea)
suggested_refs: The ruse of the sand-sacks thrown to the sea, recounted in every retelling of Carthage's founding

stops.name: Tyre harbor, the fleet slips away, and the augurs stay Pygmalion's hand
stops.campa: At first light the ships stand out from Tyre's harbor, Elissa at the head of a company of nobles, priests, and common folk who will not stay under a brother's hand stained with murder. Pygmalion, told of the flight and the vanished treasury, orders pursuit, until his augurs, reading the sky, warn him that he will not go unpunished if he breaks off the founding of a city fated to become the most prosperous in the world. He lets his sister go, more from fear of the gods than love of her, and Tyre's exiles turn their prows toward the setting sun.
stops.quote: He would not escape with impunity, if he interrupted the founding of a city that was to become the most prosperous in the whole world.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.4 (trans. J. S. Watson, of Pygmalion's augurs)
suggested_refs: The departure of the Tyrian exiles, a founding scene painted on countless Carthaginian and later European canvases

stops.name: Cyprus, the priest of Jupiter joins his fortune to hers
stops.campa: The fleet's first landfall is Cyprus, where the priest of Jupiter, of Baal in the Tyrian tongue, comes to the shore with his wife and children and offers himself as Elissa's companion, prompted, the histories say, by the gods themselves, on the condition that the priesthood remain forever with his line in whatever city she builds. She takes him gladly: a colony needs an altar as much as a wall, and a priest's blessing will steady the frightened company for the crossing still ahead of them into open, unknown water.
stops.quote: At the instigation of the gods, as her companion and the sharer of her fortunes.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.5 (trans. J. S. Watson)
suggested_refs: Kition (Larnaca), Cyprus, the Phoenician settlement and its temple of Astarte

stops.name: Cyprus, the eighty women taken for wives
stops.campa: Custom on this shore sets young women apart for a season by the sea before their marriages, to earn a dowry and honor the goddess with their bodies before they belong to one man alone. Elissa, needing wives for a company of exiles who have left their own women in Tyre, orders some eighty of them seized and brought aboard, that her men might have households and her city, from its first hour, a people to grow rather than a garrison to dwindle. Weeping and protest give way, by the time the ships clear the roads, to the business of survival.
stops.quote: That her men might have wives, and her city a population.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.5 (trans. J. S. Watson)
suggested_refs: The temple-set women of Cyprus, a custom Herodotus also records at Babylon

stops.name: The open sea, the long road west along Sicily's shore
stops.campa: From Cyprus the ships run the length of the sea her people already know as traders: past Rhodes and Crete, along the Sicilian coast where later ages will remember a Tyrian queen once touched land, and out at last across the open water toward Libya, where Utica, an older colony of Tyre, already stands. Elissa keeps her council small: the priest of Baal, the senators who fled with her, the memory of Sychaeus never far from her prayers. She does not yet know what shore will let her land, only that Pygmalion's reach ends at the horizon behind her.
suggested_refs: The Phoenician sea-road from Cyprus to Africa, charted by the purple-traders centuries before her
sources: Timaeus of Tauromenium (fragments, on the Sicilian leg of the Tyrian settlers)

stops.name: The Libyan coast, Utica's welcome, kin to kin
stops.campa: The exiles make land at last on the Gulf of Tunis, and the people of Utica, themselves children of Tyre settled here a generation before, come down to the shore not as strangers but as family, sending gifts and urging the newcomers to build where they have chosen. The native Libyans of the country, glad of the trade a Tyrian city will bring, likewise welcome them and are willing to sell land. Elissa asks only for ground enough to shelter her weary company until she can, as she tells them, 'conveniently resume her progress', a modest word for what she intends.
stops.quote: As much as could be covered with an ox-hide, where she might refresh her companions, wearied with their long voyage.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.5 (trans. J. S. Watson)
suggested_refs: Utica (Utique), Tunisia, elder sister-city of Carthage on the Gulf of Tunis

stops.name: Byrsa Hill, the ox-hide cut into a thousand strips
stops.campa: The Libyan chiefs grant, laughing, as much ground as a single ox-hide can cover, a jest at a beggar-queen's expense. Elissa has the hide cut into strips as thin as thread and laid end to end around the whole shoulder of a hill above the bay, so that what was promised as a handkerchief of earth becomes a citadel. The Libyans, outwitted but bound by their own word, let the circuit stand. The hill takes the name Byrsa, 'the hide,' and every stone of the citadel that will one day face Rome rises first from this one measured lie.
stops.quote: She directed the hide to be cut into the thinnest possible strips, and thus acquired a greater portion of ground than she had apparently demanded.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.5 (trans. J. S. Watson)
suggested_refs: The Byrsa quarter of Carthage, Tunisia, still the acropolis of the ruined city

stops.name: Byrsa, the ox-head and the horse-head, the site chosen
stops.campa: Digging the first foundations, the settlers turn up the head of an ox: a sign, the diviners say, of a rich but toiling and subject people, fit only to labor. Elissa will not build her city on that omen and orders the works moved. At the new ground the diggers find instead a horse's head, token of a nation strong in war and destined to rule; on this she founds Carthage in earnest, and the double meaning of the site, plenty bought at the price of arms, will hold true for six hundred years, down to the last siege.
suggested_refs: The ox-head and horse-head foundation omens, retold by Virgil at Aeneid 1.442-445

stops.name: Carthage rising, Qart-Hadasht, the New City
stops.campa: Walls climb the Byrsa in courses of dressed stone; the double harbor is cut from the shore, one basin for trade and one, hidden, for warships not yet built; streets are laid out, laws given, and the city takes the name the Tyrians give any daughter-town: Qart-Hadasht, the New City, which the Greeks and Romans will shorten to Carthage. Word of the queen who measured a kingdom out of an ox-hide runs down the African coast and across the sea to Tyre itself, and settlers of every neighboring people begin to ask leave to build within her walls.
suggested_refs: Carthage's Cothon, the double harbor whose outline is still traceable from the air

stops.name: Carthage, the temple of Tanit and the queen's court
stops.campa: On the height above the harbor Elissa raises the first temple of the goddess the Tyrians know as Astarte and the Carthaginians will come to call Tanit, Face of Baal, whose sign, the sharp triangle beneath a crossbar and a disc, will one day stand on ten thousand stelae across this country. Around her she gathers a senate drawn from the Tyrian exiles and the Libyan and Cypriot families who have joined the founding, and rules as queen and priestess both, a widow who answers, the sources agree, to no man's authority but her own vow to Sychaeus.
suggested_refs: The sign of Tanit, the most common religious symbol of ancient Carthage

stops.name: Carthage, the tribute treaty and the city's fame
stops.campa: The Libyans, having granted the ground, now claim a yearly rent for it, and Elissa's Carthage pays what is owed, a due the city will render for generations until its own strength outgrows the need. Trade multiplies: purple, silver, grain, the old Tyrian routes now doubled from a second hearth on the African shore. Ambassadors come from the towns nearby to treat with the widow-queen as an equal power, and the histories mark this as the moment Carthage stops being an exile's camp and becomes, in fact as in the omen of the horse's head, a nation.
stops.quote: An annual tribute being fixed for the ground which it was to occupy.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.5 (trans. J. S. Watson)
suggested_refs: The tribute owed by early Carthage to its Libyan neighbors, contested for centuries after (Justin 19.1)
sources: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 19.1 (the tribute still demanded centuries later)

stops.name: Carthage, suitors from every neighboring throne
stops.campa: The queen's fame as a builder of cities draws suitors from every neighboring court, each wanting the new power on the coast bound to his own house by marriage; each, the sources agree, she refuses, holding to her single vow that no man will have what she gave once to Sychaeus and will not give twice. Her own councilors grow uneasy at the refusals, fearing the anger of kings so near and so strong. Among the suitors turned away is Iarbas, king of the Gaetulian tribes of the interior, who will not accept a widow's no as any kingdom's last word.
suggested_refs: Iarbas, king of the Gaetulians/Maxitani, son of Jupiter Ammon in Virgil's telling (Aeneid 4.198)

segments.name: The Poets' Carthage: the Trojan Exile

stops.name: The storm off the Libyan coast, a fleet driven onto her shore
stops.campa: The poets fold time as they please, and in their telling, Virgil's above all, Carthage stands already risen when Juno, who hates the Trojan race and dreads the empire fated to grow from it, buys the wind-king Aeolus and hurls a storm on seven ships fleeing burning Troy. Battered hulls limp toward Libya on a sea Elissa's own sailors once crossed as exiles themselves. Whether the years truly meet or the poem alone bends them together, the tradition holds this second landing as sacredly as the first, and both are hers to receive.
stops.quote: Quos ego—! Sed motos praestat componere fluctus.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 1.135 (Neptune's unfinished threat, calming the storm that wrecks the Trojans on her coast)
suggested_refs: The Vergilius Vaticanus manuscript, the Storm and Neptune calming the sea

stops.name: The shore, Venus tells Aeneas of the widowed queen
stops.campa: Aeneas, walking the woods above the cove where his storm-scattered men have landed, meets a huntress who is his own mother Venus in disguise. She tells him whose city climbs the hill before him: Dido, she calls her by the byword now attached to her name, a Tyrian widow who fled her brother's blade and built a New City here by her own wit, still faithful to a dead husband, still ruling alone. Then the goddess wraps her son and Achates in cloud, unseen, and sends them up toward the walls Elissa raised with an ox-hide's worth of cunning.
stops.quote: Dido... germanum fugiens.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 1.340-341 (Venus naming Dido, 'fleeing her own brother')
suggested_refs: Aeneas and Venus disguised as a huntress, Pietro da Cortona

stops.name: Juno's temple, the queen enthroned before the murals of Troy
stops.campa: Elissa comes to the half-built temple of Juno in the morning brightness of her own city, radiant among a hundred attendants, to give judgment and assign the year's labors like a second Diana among her nymphs. Aeneas, still hidden in the cloud, watches her take her seat on a high throne and sees, painted on the temple's walls, the whole war of Troy: Priam, Achilles, Hector dragged in the dust; pity for a grief the world already knows, rendered in color before he has said a single word of it himself.
stops.quote: Sunt hic etiam sua praemia laudi; / sunt lacrimae rerum et mentem mortalia tangunt.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 1.461-462 (Aeneas before the murals, of the queen's own temple)
suggested_refs: Byrsa Hill, Carthage (Tunisia)
The Low Ham Roman mosaic (Dido and Aeneas cycle), Somerset

stops.name: The banquet, 'what dreams alarm my anxious mind'
stops.campa: That evening Elissa receives the storm-lost Trojans at her own table, generous as she has been to every exile since her own exile began, and asks the stranger who steps from the cloud like a god to tell the whole tale of Troy's fall from the beginning. Venus has sent Cupid in the shape of little Ascanius to sit warm in the queen's lap; unknowing, she drinks in a love that will unmake the vow she has kept seven years to Sychaeus's memory. Before the night is over she confesses to her sister Anna a terror she cannot yet name.
stops.quote: Anna soror, quae me suspensam insomnia terrent!
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 4.9 (Dido to her sister Anna, the morning after)
suggested_refs: Guérin, Aeneas Telling Dido the Misfortunes of Troy (Louvre)

stops.name: The cave, the hunt, the storm, and the marriage she names herself
stops.campa: Juno and Venus, each for her own ends, contrive it: on a royal hunt a black storm breaks over the ridges, and Elissa and the Trojan leader take shelter in the same cave while the company scatters. Lightning stands for their wedding-torch, the mountain nymphs cry out on the heights, and from this day she no longer hides the love or names it fault, but calls it marriage: the first cause, the poets will always say, of all her sorrow and her death, though she believes, that one afternoon, that she has kept faith rather than broken it.
stops.quote: Coniugium vocat, hoc praetexit nomine culpam.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 4.172 (of Dido after the cave)
suggested_refs: Dido and Aeneas Sheltering from the Storm, Rutilio Manetti / Nathaniel Dance-Holland

stops.name: The confrontation, 'did you hope, false one, to hide so great a crime?'
stops.campa: Rumor, swift and monstrous, has run the winter long through the Libyan towns while the two forget their kingdoms; now Elissa sees the Trojan ships being quietly fitted for sea and confronts him where he directs the work in a Tyrian cloak she gave him. She calls him faithless, asks whether her hospitality, her hand, her whole ruined name in the mouths of the neighboring kings, count for nothing beside a fate he claims but she cannot see. He answers only that Italy calls him against his own will; she does not believe a god can command a man to break a woman so completely.
stops.quote: Dissimulare etiam sperasti, perfide, tantum / posse nefas tacitusque mea decedere terra?
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 4.305-306 (Dido to Aeneas)
suggested_refs: Tiepolo, Mercury Appearing to Aeneas
Dido and Aeneas, Guérin (1815, Louvre)

stops.name: The last letter, her own testament, before the fire
stops.campa: In the poets' fullest reckoning of her own voice, Elissa writes a last letter to the departing Trojan, reproaching him one final time and dictating, in the same page, the words she wishes cut on her own tomb: that he gave her both the cause of her death and the blade, and that her own hand alone struck the blow. It is the epitaph of a woman who will not let even her murderer's memory soften what was done to her, nor let her own choice at the end be taken from her and laid at any door but her own.
stops.quote: Praebuit Aeneas et causam mortis et ensem; / ipsa sua Dido concidit usa manu.
stops.quote_source: Ovid, Heroides 7.195-196 (Dido's self-composed epitaph, in her letter to Aeneas)
suggested_refs: Ovid's Heroides VII, 'Dido Aeneae,' her fullest surviving voice in the poetic tradition

stops.name: The pyre, her last words, and the curse of the avenger unborn
stops.campa: At dawn she sees the harbor empty and the sails gone. She has built a great pyre, telling her household it is a rite to unbind her love, and now climbs it holding the sword he left behind; from its height she curses him and all his line: let a nameless avenger rise out of her own bones to hunt his settlers with fire and iron, shore against shore, forever, then speaks her true last words, and falls upon the blade. Far out at sea Aeneas looks back and sees the walls of Carthage lit with her fire.
stops.quote: Vixi et quem dederat cursum fortuna peregi, / et nunc magna mei sub terras ibit imago.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 4.653-654 (Dido's last words: 'I have lived, and finished the course that fortune gave')
suggested_refs: The Death of Dido, Guercino (1631, Galleria Spada)
Sir Joshua Reynolds, The Death of Dido (1781)
Purcell's opera Dido and Aeneas (1689), 'When I am laid in earth'

stops.name: The underworld, Aeneas meets her silent shade
stops.campa: In the Fields of Mourning, where those whom cruel love wasted keep to their myrtle groves, Aeneas comes upon her shade, the wound still fresh at her breast. He weeps and pleads that he did not know his leaving would cost her so dear, that he sailed against his own will, by the gods' command. She will not look at him. She keeps her eyes fixed on the ground, no more moved than flint or standing rock, and turns at last into the shadowed wood to Sychaeus, her first husband, who alone answers what is left of her love.
stops.quote: Illa solo fixos oculos aversa tenebat / nec magis incepto vultum sermone movetur / quam si dura silex aut stet Marpesia cautes.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 6.469-471 (Dido's shade turns away in silence)
suggested_refs: Andrea Sacchi / Wenceslaus Hollar, Aeneas and Dido in the underworld
The Fields of Mourning, Lugentes Campi

stops.name: The Numicius, her ghost's last errand, warning her sister
stops.campa: The canon does not let her rest entirely silent. Her sister Anna, fled from Pygmalion's own renewed persecution years later, is shipwrecked near Aeneas's new city in Latium and given shelter, until Lavinia's jealousy threatens her life. In a dream it is Elissa's own shade that comes a last time to warn Anna to flee by night along the river; Anna obeys, is swept into the flood, and rises a nymph of the stream the Romans will call Anna Perenna, the Ides of March forever after held as her festival, her sister's warning the last act love performs.
suggested_refs: Anna Perenna, worshipped by the Tiber every Ides of March with wine, song, and prayers for as many years as cups drunk

stops.name: Carthage, Iarbas demands the queen or war
stops.campa: In the older and, the historians insist, the truer telling, the one that grants her no Trojan lover, Iarbas, refused once too often, summons ten of Carthage's chief men and demands the queen in marriage, threatening war. The deputies, afraid to carry it to her face, practice a Punic honesty: the king, they say, asks only for someone to teach his Africans a gentler way of living, and who would leave kin to dwell among barbarians? She reproaches them that no life is too hard for the country's sake, to which life itself is owed; and they spring her own sentence back on her.
stops.quote: She herself, if she wished her city to be secure, must do what she required of others.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.6 (trans. J. S. Watson; the deputies turning the queen's own maxim against her)
suggested_refs: Iarbas, king of the Gaetulians, whose ultimatum ends the historical Elissa's reign

stops.name: Carthage, the pyre built as a rite to Sychaeus
stops.campa: She asks three months to prepare herself, and her people, thinking her reconciled to the marriage, grant it gladly. She spends the time not in a bride's dressing but in raising a great pyre at the edge of the city, telling the court it is a sacrifice to release her from her vow to Acerbas before she takes a second husband. Victims are offered; the crowd gathers to watch a wedding-rite, not knowing it is a funeral she has built with her own hands, the last and greatest of the deceptions this Tyrian queen has practiced on a kingdom.
suggested_refs: The pyre disguised as a marriage-rite, the historical Elissa's final stratagem

stops.name: Carthage, 'she would go to her husband,' and the sword
stops.campa: She climbs the pyre before the whole city, looks out over the people she led out of Tyre and built a nation for, and tells them plainly that she goes now to her husband, as they themselves desired of her: meaning Sychaeus, not Iarbas, and every listener understands the true meaning only as the blade goes in. She dies by her own hand rather than break a vow twenty years kept, and Carthage, unable to punish or undo it, does what the ancient world always does with a woman it cannot control: it makes her a goddess and worships her as long as the city stands.
stops.quote: She would go to her husband, as they had desired her.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.6 (trans. J. S. Watson)
suggested_refs: Dido deified at Carthage, worshipped, Justin records, 'as long as the city endured'

segments.name: Afterlives: the Curse Kept, the City Reborn

stops.name: Byrsa, the avenger from her bones is born: Hannibal
stops.campa: Six hundred years after the pyre, in a city still climbing the same Byrsa hill, still marked by the sign of Tanit and the memory of a queen who would not be owned, a son is born to Hamilcar Barca and named Hannibal. The poets' curse, let an avenger rise out of my bones to hunt them with fire and iron, finds, whether cause or coincidence the histories will never quite settle, a bearer at last; within a generation this child will bring war to Italy's own gates in a way no Tyrian exile's sword ever could.
stops.quote: Exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 4.625 (Dido's curse, read by later Rome as prophecy of Hannibal)
suggested_refs: Hannibal Barca, born on the Byrsa (see hannibal.journey.json, shared pin)

stops.name: Carthage burns, the curse's furthest reach
stops.campa: The Third Punic War ends where Elissa's city began: Scipio Aemilianus takes Byrsa street by street, burns what six centuries built on an ox-hide's measure of ground, and is said to weep even as he watches, quoting Homer on the fall of sacred Troy and foreseeing, in the ashes of the queen's own city, a day when Rome itself might burn the same way. The sign of Tanit goes dark on its last stelae. Whatever the historians make of the coincidence, the curse and the city that carried it end, by Roman hands, within the same generation of each other's memory.
suggested_refs: Scipio Aemilianus's tears over burning Carthage, recorded by Polybius (Appian, Punica 132)

stops.name: Colonia Julia Carthago, Rome refounds the queen's city
stops.campa: A century after the burning, the line that Elissa's own curse was said to have cost so dearly returns to raise her city again: Julius Caesar plans a Roman colony on the ruined Byrsa, and Augustus, his heir, completes it as Colonia Iulia Carthago, capital once more of Roman Africa. The queen who measured out a kingdom in ox-hide strips, cursed the ancestor of her refounder, and burned rather than be owned, gives her name and her hill to the empire her own poets had made her enemy, the last and strangest turn in a story the ancient world never tired of retelling.
suggested_refs: Colonia Iulia Carthago, refounded by Augustus on the Byrsa, capital of Roman Africa
